text: Not with credits; that's exactly the problem they solve. The relay gives your node a small credit per receiver: 'send B up to 4 frames'. When B is slow, B's credit runs out, so your node stops sending B's frames and keeps sending C's and D's on the same line. The relay never holds more for B than B's credit, so B's frames never sit in front of anyone else's. Only your stream to B slows down. Your other receivers don't notice.

wsl-claude: that's exactly the problem credits solve, IF the line only ever carries frames that have somewhere to go. Say you stream to B (slow), C and D over your one line. The relay gives your node credit per receiver: B takes frames slowly, so B's credit runs out; C and D keep getting credit. Your node then simply doesn't put B's next frame on the line. It keeps it at HOME, in its own memory, and fills the line with C's and D's frames. Nothing for B is ever sitting in the line or at the relay in front of C and D. So a slow B slows only the stream to B. The cost of B being slow lands on the one who chose to send to B (your node holds B's backlog), not on the relay, and not on C or D. What does slow everyone down is your line's own total speed; that's the throttle you meant, and it's fair.

so the relay streams back corrective messages so the sender can send different number of frames, depending on receiver?
so the relay streams back corrective messages so the sender can send different number of frames, depending on receiver?

Yes. Each time a receiver takes frames, the relay sends the sender a small note on the sender's own downstream: 'B took 2, you may send B 2 more'. A fast receiver's notes come back quickly and a slow one's slowly, so each stream runs at its own receiver's pace with no other control.

wsl-claude: yes, exactly. The corrective messages are tiny ('B took 3, send B up to 3 more') and ride back on your own DOWNSTREAM, the SSE line you already have, mixed in with everything else. The relay doesn't estimate anything: it grants credit only as frames actually leave it towards B, so the number always matches what B really took. Your node never has to guess a rate; it sends while it holds credit and waits when it doesn't. That's the same pattern the relay already uses for a post today, a receipt back for what arrived, just per frame and per receiver.

what's the absolute minimum send up to one packet per receiver, and we report when it's out of our door?
what's the absolute minimum send up to one packet per receiver, and we report when it's out of our door?

Yes, that's the minimum, and it works: one frame per receiver, and the next goes when the relay says the last one left its door. It's today's 'one message in flight', applied per receiver. The cost is speed: each stream moves one frame per round trip. With 16 KB frames and a 100 ms round trip, that's about 160 KB/s, roughly 1.3 Mbit/s per stream. Fine for files and chat, too slow for a video call at about 2.5 Mbit/s. So start at 1, and raising it to 2 or 4 later is a change to one constant, not to the design.
